concepts.title: How Many Days' Wages Would Cover the Basics?
concepts.selected_technique: Large readable focal point plus local contrast; one oversized paper wage token marked 333 beside a small necessities basket. The numeral is the evidence hook, with the basket supplying its referent.
concepts.brief: A richly layered handmade paper/card diorama: one large, tactile paper wage token stamped ‘333’ dominates the foreground, balanced against a compact basket containing bread, folded linen, a soap bar, candle and fuel. A small London labourer figure looks from the token to the basket, giving the objects human scale without implying a specific documented family. Warm amber light isolates the token and basket against a simplified deep blue-brown paper background. Add the short large cut-paper headline ‘333 WORKDAYS?’ in wide rounded irregular paper letters with thickness and soft physical shadow. Clear silhouette and high local contrast; three or four major groups; no tiny labels, no modern money, no photorealistic person, no decorative frame. Honest editorial reconstruction, not an archival scene.
concepts.visual_intent: Make the surprising length of the model's wage-day cost instantly legible, while showing that 333 refers to a defined basic-needs basket. Preserve uncertainty with a question mark; do not imply an observed time sheet or universal family budget.
concepts.audience_interest: A striking number turns a familiar question about necessities into a tangible scale-of-work puzzle.
concepts.genre_mood: Historical investigation; curious, grounded, slightly tense.
concepts.first_confirmation: Opening hook: before the Black Death the model basket costs about 333 wage-days, while the assumed year has 250 paid days; the annual wage falls short.
concepts.payoff: Resolution and final section explain the later 116-day estimate and carefully bound what the remainder can mean.
concepts.likely_misreading_and_mitigation: ‘333 workdays’ could be mistaken for a documented annual work schedule or a modern household measure. The question mark, visible basket, and description's explicit model/reconstruction caveat keep the claim bounded.
concepts.description:
Bread. Fuel. Soap. Candles. How much work did a year's basic necessities cost a London labourer's family?

This film compares selected London labourer wage estimates with a reconstructed annual basket of basic needs for a family of four, from before the Black Death to the late nineteenth century. The basket includes food, linen, soap, candles, fuel and a small housing allowance. Its wage-day figures are a model for comparison, not surviving records of anyone's working year or a measure of every family's spending.

The answer changes across the centuries: the basket is estimated at about 333 days' pay before the Black Death, around 176 days in 1500–1549, about 216 days in 1600–1649, and approximately 116 days in 1850–1899. The film follows the surprising reversal when daily wages rose but prices rose faster, and explains what a lower wage-day cost can—and cannot—tell us about basic purchasing power.

#EconomicHistory #CostOfLiving #LondonHistory #PaperDetour

concepts.title: When Wages Doubled, Why Did the Basics Cost More?
concepts.selected_technique: Visible before/after transformation with a strong directional relationship; contrast is in the wage and price movement, not merely a split-color treatment.
concepts.brief: A continuous handmade paper/card diorama, not a generic split screen: on the left a modest silver wage stack grows across a raised paper bridge into a visibly taller stack on the right, while the necessities basket below becomes heavier and its hanging paper price tag rises even higher. A single London labourer figure points between the changed wage and the rising basket. Place a bold cut-paper ‘PAY ↑ / COST ↑↑’ headline across open space in rounded, irregular dimensional letters. Directional folds and shadows guide the eye from wage to basket; warm and cool local light distinguish growth without implying precise silver quantities or an exact single transaction. Simplify background; no modern currency symbols or chart UI.
concepts.visual_intent: Represent the film's reversal: a larger daily wage does not guarantee a cheaper basic-needs basket when prices rise faster.
concepts.audience_interest: An apparent contradiction invites viewers to discover why nominal pay and purchasing power diverge.
concepts.first_confirmation: Hook establishes the later reversal; the investigation gives the early 1500s benchmark of about 176 wage-days and asks viewers to predict what happens after the silver wage more than doubles.
concepts.payoff: Climax: the basket rises from about 176 to about 216 wage-days as the price index outpaces the silver wage.
concepts.likely_misreading_and_mitigation: Could imply the entire wage increase was lost or that every price rose identically. The description and film specify a reconstructed basket and compare aggregate estimates for two selected periods.
concepts.description:
A daily wage can rise sharply while basic necessities become harder to cover. How?

This film compares selected London building-labourer wage estimates with a reconstructed annual basic-needs basket for a family of four. Across the early 1500s and early 1600s, the estimated silver wage more than doubles, yet the basket rises from about 176 to about 216 days' pay because prices grow faster than wages.

The basket includes food, linen, soap, candles, fuel and a small housing allowance. These are modelled wage-day equivalents, not records of anyone's actual working year or a complete account of household spending. The film traces the comparison from before the Black Death to 1850–1899, when the basket is estimated at approximately 116 days' pay.

#EconomicHistory #HistoricalWages #CostOfLiving #PaperDetour

concepts.title: When Did a Year of Necessities Take Fewer Workdays?
concepts.selected_technique: Threshold/contrast as a material paper cutaway: the same basket crosses a visible line of wage-days at two points in the story.
concepts.brief: A single handmade paper/card diorama built around a deep cutaway staircase of wage-day tokens. The same miniature necessities basket sits on a high ledge labelled only by the large cut-paper number ‘333’ at one end and a lower ledge ‘116 DAYS’ at the other; a curved paper path connects the two, suggesting comparison over time rather than a single household's journey. A small labourer figure stands at the threshold between the levels, looking toward the lower basket. Use bold depth, tactile torn edges and physical shadows, with the ‘116 DAYS’ headline as the dominant readable element. No false precision beyond the stated approximate figures; no modern graph interface, no extra dates in tiny text.
concepts.visual_intent: Offer a long-range change-over-time question focused on how the model basket's wage-day cost later falls, distinct from A's initial shortfall and B's price-versus-pay reversal.
concepts.audience_interest: A large visual distance between 333 and 116 asks what changed across centuries.
concepts.genre_mood: Long-view historical inquiry; reflective, hopeful but measured.
concepts.first_confirmation: Hook gives the 333-day pre-Black-Death estimate; resolution introduces the approximately 116-day estimate for 1850–1899.
concepts.payoff: The resolution explains the lower relative basket cost and explicitly limits what the remaining earnings can establish about leisure, savings, or actual household budgets.
concepts.likely_misreading_and_mitigation: A descending stair could imply a smooth, steady improvement. The image connects only two selected points and the title asks when; the film explicitly notes an intervening rise from 176 to 216 days.
concepts.description:
The same basic-needs yardstick gives very different answers across selected periods of London history.

This film follows a reconstructed annual basket for a family of four—from food, linen, soap, candles and fuel to a small housing allowance—and compares its estimated cost with selected labourer wages. It is about the price of this defined basket in days' pay, not every family's spending or a surviving work calendar.

The comparison begins at about 333 wage-days before the Black Death, falls to around 176 in 1500–1549, rises to about 216 in 1600–1649, and reaches approximately 116 in 1850–1899. The path is not a steady decline: the film shows why a faster rise in prices could outweigh a growing daily wage, and what the later lower figure does—and does not—tell us.

#LondonHistory #EconomicHistory #CostOfLiving #PaperDetour
